paper_title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required effects. To address this completion gap, we propose Interlock, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects. Interlock compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements. To evaluate training utility, we fine-tune two Qwen3.6 backbones on their own accepted trajectories. Across the two backbones, training improves AutomationBench task pass rates by 4.00-4.50 percentage points, JobBench weighted scores by 3.20-6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rates by 3.89-4.16 percentage points. These results demonstrate the training utility of the synthesized experience across external task environments.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Long-horizon agents increasingly work with records, rules, resources, and partially completed artifacts. short request can require reconciling conflicting evidence, determining which objects need attention, selecting feasible plan, and updating several related results. The environment supplies the facts and constraints that determine this work. decision can also activate further obligations: deferring an action may require an explanation and handoff, while changing an allocation may require corresponding revisions to schedules and budgets. These obligations can outlive the interaction in which they are discovered: after many intervening reads, computations, and edits, the agent must still apply the earlier evidence and decisions to every affected result. Local progress can coexist with an incomplete outcome (Figure 1). correct decision can leave necessary consequences unfulfilled, and mutually consistent outputs can share an unsupported assumption. These failures concern the relationships that connect evidence, decisions, and the requested outcome. They motivate our central question: how can task synthesis preserve conditional obligations and turn their fulfillment into transferable training experience? Equal contribution. Corresponding authors. 1 Figure 1: From local correctness to task completion. correct flight booking can still leave schedule and budget updates unfinished. INTERLOCK preserves grounding, coupling, and realization relations during task synthesis to connect evidence, decisions, and required downstream effects. We characterize this structure as typed completion graph. Grounding connects environmental evidence and rules to the decisions they support. Coupling links components that must share feasible choice or satisfy joint constraint. Realization connects decision to every downstream record, artifact, or state that must reflect it. Their interaction is especially demanding over long executions: an early finding can constrain work completed many interactions later, and revised decision can require coordinated changes to several existing artifacts. Task synthesis and environment generation provide scalable basis for agent training. Prior work constructs verified tool-use data (Qin et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024), generates environments and task scenarios (Hu et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026), and composes extended tasks through tool dependencies and reusable workflows (Tu et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). Common specifications can also align instructions, environments, and verifiers (Ivanov & Rana, 2026). Our organizing unit is the complete set of conditional obligations for an outcome. It determines both the unresolved work placed in an environment and the evidence needed to accept the result. We propose INTERLOCK to make this graph an explicit synthesis constraint. Reusable domain descriptions and archetype contracts define evidence roles, task-specific decisions and shared states, joint conditions, and downstream consumers. Three generation roles compile the same graph into workspace, task/contract, and rubric while leaving concrete associations and decisions to the agent. source-coverage review traces every typed relation from the original graph through these artifacts; public-input critic independently checks whether the resulting criteria are supported by solvervisible materials and assessable from execution artifacts. Completion-filtered training then selects executions that realize every applicable effect. Our evaluation connects task structure, execution behavior, and training utility. Statistical analyses and case studies examine dependencies and completion failures. The training protocol uses Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B separately, retaining each models own accepted rollouts for SFT of that same model. Both backbones improve on AutomationBench, JobBench Main and Easy, and Harvey LAB. Gains over the original checkpoints reach 4.004.50 percentage points in AutomationBench task pass rate, 3.206.64 points in JobBench weighted score, and 3.894.16 percentage points in Harvey LAB criterion pass rate. These results show that experience from complete synthetic executions transfers to independently authored tasks across different environments. Our contributions are threefold: typed representation of task completion. We model long-horizon tasks as completion graphs whose grounding, coupling, and realization relations connect public evidence, consequential decisions, joint constraints, and required effects. 2 Graph-grounded synthesis and review. We compile the same graph into the environment, task specification, deliverable contract, and outcome criteria, with complementary reviews for source coverage and public support. Empirical validation of training utility. We evaluate the generated experience through completion-filtered fine-tuning of two backbones and measure transfer across three external benchmarks.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Task synthesis and environment generation provide scalable source of agent experience. ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023), ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2024), and ToolACE (Liu et al., 2025) broaden tool coverage and interaction diversity, while APIGen (Liu et al., 2024) incorporates format, execution, and semantic verification. Beyond tool-use data, AgentGen (Hu et al., 2025), AutoForge (Cai et al., 2025), and EnvScaler (Song et al., 2026) extend synthesis to environments and their associated planning tasks or executable scenarios. Agent-World (Dong et al., 2026) further couples environmenttask discovery with self-evolving training, and ClawGym (Bai et al., 2026) brings synthesis to persistent workspaces through persona-driven intents, skill-grounded operations, and hybrid verification. To construct extended interactions, ToolFlow (Wang et al., 2025) plans coherent tool-use dialogues, while APIGen-MT (Prabhakar et al., 2026) turns verified action blueprints into multi-turn interactions. BUTTON (Chen et al., 2025), TaskCraft (Shi et al., 2026), and AgentSynth (Xie et al., 2026) construct complex requests by composing or expanding smaller tasks. Complementary approaches, including VOYAGER (Wang et al., 2023), OS-Genesis (Sun et al., 2025), and Explorer (Pahuja et al., 2025), obtain curricula or tasks through environmental state and exploration. Alongside task complexity, another line of work addresses consistency among generated instructions, environments, and verifiers. Endless Terminals (Gandhi et al., 2026) generates containerized tasks with completion tests, while RST (Li et al., 2026b) extends verified reference solutions and realigns instructions and verifiers with the resulting workflows. CodeMidas (Ye et al., 2026) derives coding tasks from existing implementations, grounds synthesized tests in execution of the original code, and filters tasks through execution checks and agent rollouts. Anchor (Ivanov & Rana, 2026) addresses artifact drift by deriving task artifacts and certified solutions from common constraint program. Graphguided synthesis provides more explicit control over the dependencies underlying generated tasks. ScaleEnv (Tu et al., 2026) constructs tasks from tested tool dependencies, EnvFactory (Xu et al., 2026b) uses topology-aware sampling to generate grounded queries, and SkillSynth (Fan et al., 2026) instantiates paths through scenario-mediated skill graph. These approaches organize generation around tool connectivity and skill relationships. INTERLOCK instead uses task-completion relationships as synthesis constraints: its typed completion graph grounds decisions in evidence, imposes joint constraints, and specifies required downstream effects.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Models and training. We use Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the base models and consider the following three settings: the original checkpoint, ClawGym-SFT on released demonstrations (Bai et al., 2026), and Interlock-RFT on each backbones own accepted rollouts. Both backbones use thinking mode during training and evaluation. The reported corpus retains 3,278 tasks with at least one accepted rollout from each backbone. Five attempts per task and backbone yield 32,780 attempts, of which 32,370 terminate normally. Each Interlock-RFT model uses 8,957 of its own accepted trajectories and approximately 154M supervised tokens, including reasoning, responses, and tool calls. Benchmarks and metrics. We evaluate on AutomationBench (600 public tasks) (Shepard & Salimans, 2026), JobBench Main and Easy (65 tasks each) (Li et al., 2026a), and Harvey LAB (1,251 public tasks) (Harvey AI, 2026). These evaluation instances are excluded from synthesis and RFT. The respective metrics are task pass rate, task-averaged weighted score, and criterion pass rate, all on 0100 scale with higher values better. JobBench runs in OpenCode, and GPT-5.5 judges both JobBench and Harvey LAB. Each backbone is trained on its own accepted trajectories, and the gains extend across coordinated API execution, professional deliverables, and legal work. For Qwen3.6-27B, INTERLOCK improves AutomationBench task pass rate by 4.00 percentage points, JobBench Main and Easy weighted scores by 4.35 and 6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rate by 3.89 percentage points over the original checkpoint. For Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the gains are 4.50 percentage points on AutomationBench, 3.20 and 4.31 score points on JobBench Main and Easy, and 4.16 percentage points on Harvey LAB. The improvements therefore cover task completion on AutomationBench, weighted rubric fulfillment on JobBench, and criterion satisfaction on Harvey LAB. 4.3 TASK DIVERSITY AND TRANSFER We vary the number of training domains over 16, 32, 64, and 128. All four Interlock-RFT settings use 8,957 training trajectories, matching the Qwen3.6-27B main experiment. Tasks are grouped by domain, with each domain containing task families that share business or professional context (Section 3.2). Domain coverage therefore measures the breadth of professional settings represented in training. Performance increases at every successive setting on all four metrics, with 128 domains achieving the highest values. At fixed trajectory count, broader domain coverage supplies more varied instances of these completion requirements. sections.title: 4.4 AGENTIC VERIFICATION FOR COMPLETION-FILTERED TRAINING
sections.content: We compare two trajectory judges on Qwen3.6-27B to isolate the training contribution of the trajectory judge. Both judging configurations use the same judge backbone, public task requests, rubrics, and acceptance rule (Section 3.4) to filter the fixed rollout pool underlying the Qwen3.6-27B Interlock-RFT result. The text-only LLM-as-judge receives fixed textual representation of the initial and final workspaces and their diff, while the agent-as-judge can inspect the same snapshots and write and execute verification scripts. The agent-filtered condition reuses the main Interlock-RFT checkpoint. The text-filtered condition is fine-tuned from the same initial Qwen3.6-27B checkpoint with the same optimization settings. Verification output counts all judge-generated tokens, including verification-script and tool-call tokens, summed over all verification calls for each candidate rollout and averaged over the entire pool. Tool-returned content is excluded from this output count. Agent-based filtering improves all four downstream metrics at the matched training budget  (Table 2)  . Average judge output increases from approximately 11.03k to 12.28k tokens per candidate rollout, an 11.3% increase, or about 1.25k additional tokens. These gains support checking submitted artifacts through inspection and recomputation when selecting demonstrations for task completion. With the rollout pool, judge backbone, and supervision budget held fixed, executable verification improves the training value of the selected trajectories. 4.5 LONG-HORIZON EXECUTION ON SYNTHESIZED TASKS The 3,278 retained tasks each receive five rollout attempts from Qwen3.6-27B and five from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, giving 32,780 attempts. Excluding 410 non-normal executions leaves 32,370 trajectories for execution-horizon analysis. Each backbone selects 8,957 of its own accepted trajectories for training, with approximately 154M supervised tokens in each training set. We characterize execution horizon over this normally terminated pool through assistant turns, tool calls, and recorded trajectory tokens. Figure 4 compares the 32,370 normally terminated INTERLOCK trajectories with 24,497 released ClawGym trajectories. INTERLOCK trajectories average 84,293 recorded tokens, 27.63 assistant turns, and 42.10 tool calls, compared with 14,940 tokens, 11.92 turns, and 14.76 calls for ClawGym. The corresponding ratios are 5.64, 2.32, and 2.85. The difference extends to the centers of the distributions: median assistant turns are 25 versus 9, and median tool calls are 40 versus 12. Appendix specifies the population and counting rules and provides the cumulative distributions and histograms. Assistant turns measure successive model responses, while tool calls measure the actions submitted during those responses. Their joint increase grounds the long-horizon characterization in repeated interaction with the task environment. These execution statistics show that INTERLOCK produces tasks that elicit sustained agent work, providing experience in carrying evidence, decisions, and required effects across many interactions. Appendix gives the measurement protocol. 4.6 GENERALIZATION ACROSS TASK ENVIRONMENTS Figure 5 visualizes selected public task statements JobBench from INTERLOCK, AutomationBench, Main, and Harvey LAB. We encode each statement with BGE-M3 (Chen et al., 2024) and project the normalized embeddings into two dimensions using PCA followed by t-SNE (Van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008). INTERLOCK tasks span broad area of the projection and form multiple dispersed groups, reflecting diverse task content. This breadth extends to environment construction: the retained corpus covers 128 domains and 484 task families, with multi-file workspaces containing task-specific records, policies, and unfinished artifacts (Appendix D). These settings vary the evidence, joint constraints, and downstream obligations over which grounding, coupling, and realization must be satisfied. AutomationBench, JobBench, and Harvey LAB together evaluate out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer to independently authored tasks with their own materials, interfaces, and outcome requirements. Their task statements form dataset-specific groups in the projection, and their evaluation instances are excluded from synthesis and RFT. Consistent gains across all three benchmarks and both backbones  (Table 1)  demonstrate the training value of complete synthetic executions beyond the generated task distribution. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: INTERLOCK organizes long-horizon task synthesis around typed completion graphs. Grounding, coupling, and realization relations constrain how public evidence, consequential decisions, joint conditions, and required effects are compiled into task environments and outcome criteria. Dual-view review checks both graph preservation and public support, while completion-filtered RFT selects executions that realize every applicable graph effect. Training improves both Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B across AutomationBench, JobBench Main and Easy, and Harvey LAB, supporting the value of complete synthetic execution experience for transfer across task environments.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used generative AI tools to assist with prompt design and manuscript preparation, including language polishing, bilingual editing, and the preparation of figures and captions. As described in Section 3, AI agents are integral to the task synthesis and training-data collection procedure: they generate initial workspaces, task instructions, and outcome rubrics; review task requirements and quality; execute tasks; and assess the resulting artifacts. The roles and verification procedures for these agents are documented in the methodology and experimental setup. We have manually reviewed all AI-assisted work, including manuscript revisions, prompts, generated task materials, and execution and evaluation records. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including its text, analyses, claims, and artifacts produced with AI assistance.

sections.title: G ALGORITHM AND EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: G.1 TASK SYNTHESIS AND TRAINING ALGORITHM Algorithm 1 summarizes task construction, admission, and completion-filtered training. 24 G.2 DETAILED EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Models and training conditions. We evaluate INTERLOCK on two backbones, Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. For each backbone, the main experiment compares its original checkpoint, model fine-tuned on released ClawGym trajectories, and model trained with INTERLOCK through rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT). All three variants are evaluated on AutomationBench, JobBench, and Harvey LAB. The comparison examines the training value of the generated experience and its transfer to external task distributions. Appendix reports statistics of the retained task corpus, including archetype coverage, workspace and rubric size, and verification methods. Original. The original checkpoint is the starting policy before either data-based training procedure. It provides the reference for measuring the effect of additional training within each backbone. ClawGym-SFT. We directly use the trajectories released by ClawGym (Bai et al., 2026) for supervised fine-tuning of each starting model. This baseline represents training on an existing source of environment-grounded agent demonstrations. Interlock-RFT. In the proposed protocol, each backbone independently executes INTERLOCK tasks and supplies its own rollout pool. Normally ended trajectories satisfying the acceptance rule in Section 3.4 are used for SFT initialized from the same backbone. Rollout generation, acceptance, and parameter updates remain separate for Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. RFT denotes this combination of rejection sampling and SFT. Task screening and rollout accounting. The reported corpus contains 3,278 synthesized tasks retained after screening. Each retained task has at least one accepted rollout from Qwen3.6-27B and at least one from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. This criterion defines the task set used in the reported experiments. For each retained task, each backbone makes = 5 rollout attempts from reset workspaces, giving 3,278 2 5 = 32,780 attempts, or 16,390 per backbone. We exclude 410 attempts that do not terminate normally because of execution anomalies or incomplete execution, leaving 32,370 normally terminated trajectories for trajectory analysis. Normal termination concerns execution status; trajectory acceptance is determined separately by AV (x, τ ). From its own normally terminated rollout pool, Qwen3.6-27B selects 8,957 accepted trajectories for its RFT training set. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B independently selects 8,957 accepted trajectories from its own pool for its own training. The two training sets contain 17,914 trajectories in total, with approximately 154M supervised tokens per backbone (M = 106). Supervised tokens are assistantgenerated positions that contribute to the training loss, including reasoning, responses, and tool calls. System and user messages, tool-returned observations, and tool schemas provide conditioning context and are excluded from this supervision count. These conditions compare the full INTERLOCK data-generation and training procedure with both the original model and released-trajectory SFT alternative. The ClawGym baseline uses its published demonstrations, whereas INTERLOCK generates and selects demonstrations from the target backbone itself. Training-data sizes and optimization budgets are specified separately for each condition. Implementation details. Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B use the same SFT configuration in Table 3. Each model is trained for five epochs on 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs with 141 GB of memory per GPU. BENCHMARKS FOR LONG-HORIZON AGENTS Long-horizon benchmarks provide concrete settings in which successful interaction must produce the requested outcome. WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024) and OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) evaluate realistic web and desktop tasks with execution-based outcome checks. AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) tests stateful multi-application coding and unintended changes, and ToolSandbox (Lu et al., 2025) emphasizes implicit state dependencies and intermediate milestones. These settings connect task success to environmental state and applicable rules, motivating our treatment of completion as set of linked requirements. WorkArena++ (Boisvert et al., 2024) targets compositional planning and reasoning in knowledge work, while TheAgentCompany (Xu et al., 2026a) combines websites, code execution, and workplace communication. Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026) couples challenging command-line tasks with dedicated environments and tests, and Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench (Li et al., 2026c) evaluates extended workflows with graded subtasks and partial credit. Their emphasis on coordinated work and outcome evaluation complements INTERLOCKs focus on preserving completion requirements during task synthesis. Our external evaluations span three forms of consequential work. AutomationBench (Shepard & Salimans, 2026) brings together cross-application orchestration, autonomous API discovery, and layered policy compliance. JobBench (Li et al., 2026a) evaluates expert-prioritized delegations in heterogeneous reference workspaces using fact-anchored chains of binary rubric criteria. Harvey LAB (Harvey AI, 2026) evaluates legal work in document-rich matter workspaces through deliverable-specific binary criteria covering factual support, analysis, and required content. Using each benchmarks own evaluation protocol, these independently authored tasks assess the downstream value of the synthesized environments and data for agents facing new evidence, constraints, and required effects.
